# Missing abstracts, fail-open, and search narrowing

## 📋 REVISION HISTORY

This file was written in two passes on 2026-07-25. The first pass reasoned from
a simulation; a live API probe then falsified its central premise. Read this
table before quoting anything below.

| claim in pass 1 | status | what settled it |
|---|---|---|
| *"For a work with no abstract, `title_and_abstract` search reduces to the title alone"* | ❌ **FALSIFIED** | `filter=doi:10.1006/phrs.1999.0495,title_and_abstract.search:cardiovascular` returns **1 match**, although "cardiovascular" is absent from that work's title and its `abstract_inverted_index` is `null`. OpenAlex indexes abstract text it does not return. |
| Q3's 8-work *"dropped by narrowing"* list | ⚠️ **UNRELIABLE** | Computed from titles only, on the falsified premise. It understates what a narrowed search returns. Still valid as *"the title alone does not carry the intervention token"* — nothing more. |
| *"Narrowing would permanently lose 2 of the 4 works the gate gets wrong"* | ❌ **REFUTED** | Live variant C returns both the DHA and the (n-3) papers (2/3 group-B). The loss is real for variant E, but it is not a property of narrowing as such. |
| *"A synonym table is a precondition for narrowing safely"* | ❌ **WITHDRAWN, unfounded** | Variant D is exactly that shape and has the **worst** recall of all five (5/32 gate-kept works returned). ORing synonyms into the filter inflates the pool to 577 924 and destroys the top-62. |
| Q1 table (33 abstract-less works, 25 with the intervention token in the title) | ✅ **stands as measured** | Correct as a statement about titles. **It does not answer what a narrowed search returns** — see the falsified premise above. |
| Q2 list (18 works a fail-open rule would admit) | ✅ **stands** | It describes our own gate's verdicts, not OpenAlex's search. Unaffected. |
| *"`abstract_inverted_index` is null for these works, so `ReconstructAbstract` is not at fault"* | ✅ **stands** | Probed directly on three works; all null at the source. |

**Question this file answers:** 24% of works in the six benefit-shaped corpora
arrive from OpenAlex with no abstract, and they make up 35% of the PICO gate's
exclusions. Two candidate fixes compete for priority — narrowing the OpenAlex
search so less off-topic material is fetched, and backfilling abstracts from
another source. This file produces the facts needed to order them.

**Data source:** `testdata/corpora_full/` (untruncated re-export, 2026-07-25).

**Generated by:** `internal/scengine/pico_excluded_test.go` —
`TestNoAbstractQ1TitleCarriesIntervention`, `TestNoAbstractQ2FailOpenAdmits`,
`TestNoAbstractQ3NarrowingInteraction`. Run with
`go test ./internal/scengine/ -run TestNoAbstractQ -v`.

## ⚠️ How to read this file

| | |
|---|---|
| 🔵 **MEASURED** | Produced by code or by a live API call, reproducible. The Go tests compute nothing but raw facts — which work, does it have an abstract, is the intervention token in its title, is the outcome token in its title, does it pass the gate. **No classification is computed in code.** |
| 🟡 **JUDGED** | Claude's reading of those facts. Opinion, not measurement. Not expert-validated. |

The gate logic used is the existing `fixedPICOTokens` + `containsAnyToken` +
`IsPICORelevant`. No second tokenizer exists in the test file, so any difference
from earlier numbers comes from the data, never from two implementations of the
same rule drifting apart.

# 🛑 CORRECTION (added after the first version of this file)

This file was first written on a simulation premise that a later live API probe
**falsified**. The premise was:

> *"OpenAlex's title/abstract search sees title + abstract. For a work whose
> abstract is absent, that reduces to the title alone."*

**That is wrong.** OpenAlex's search index contains abstract text for works whose
`abstract_inverted_index` is `null` in the API response — the API withholds the
abstract (licensing), but still indexes it. Measured, 2026-07-25:

| probe | result |
|---|---|
| `filter=doi:10.1006/phrs.1999.0495,title_and_abstract.search:cardiovascular` | **1 match** — yet "cardiovascular" is absent from that work's title, and its `abstract_inverted_index` is `null` |
| same work, control: `…,title_and_abstract.search:docosahexaenoic` (a title word) | 1 match |
| `filter=doi:10.1038/s41591-019-0439-x,title_and_abstract.search:health` | **1 match** — "health" absent from the title, index `null` |
| `filter=doi:10.1016/j.amjmed.2014.10.014,title_and_abstract.search:omega` | 0 matches — so it is not universal |

**What still stands:** `abstract_inverted_index` really is `null` for these works
(probed directly), which is why our local JSON has an empty abstract, and which
exonerates `ReconstructAbstract` — there is no reconstruction bug. The earlier
note in this file that read "premise verified" verified only that, and was
wrongly extended to the search index. Two different systems; conflating them was
the error.

**What falls:** the Q3 split into "survives narrowing" / "dropped by narrowing"
below is computed from titles alone and therefore **understates** what a narrowed
search would return. Read Q3 as *"does the title alone carry the token"* — which
is what it measures — and not as *"would OpenAlex return this work"*. The live
variant measurement further down supersedes it for that question.

**What this cost:** the original JUDGED conclusion of this file — *"narrowing
would permanently lose two of the four works the gate gets wrong, so a synonym
table is a precondition for narrowing"* — is contradicted by direct measurement.
See the corrected section at the end.

# 🔵 MEASURED — Part 1: the OpenAlex search semantics

Everything in this section is from the OpenAlex documentation
(`developers.openalex.org/guides/searching`) or from a live API probe, not from
memory.

### From the documentation

| question | documented answer |
|---|---|
| what does `search=` cover on `/works`? | **`title`, `abstract`, `fulltext`** |
| multiple words? | *"Words not separated by boolean operators are treated as `AND`."* |
| stemming? | *"OpenAlex uses stemming and removes stop words to improve results."* |
| boolean syntax? | *"Use `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` (uppercase) … Surround phrases with double quotes for exact matching."* |
| `title_and_abstract.search`? | Not present in the current guide; the field-scoped `.search` filters are described as the deprecated approach, with `search=` recommended instead. |

### From a live API probe (2026-07-25)

OpenAlex echoes its own interpretation of every query in `meta.x_query.oql`,
which settles what each form actually does:

| query | `meta.x_query.oql` | result count |
|---|---|---:|
| `search=omega-3 improves cardiovascular health` (**what this CLI sends today**) | `works where full text has (omega-3 improves cardiovascular health)` | **76 524** |
| `filter=title_and_abstract.search:omega-3` | `works where title/abstract has (omega-3)` | 89 290 |
| `filter=title_and_abstract.search:omega-3 cardiovascular health` | `works where title/abstract has (omega-3 cardiovascular health)` | **2 933** |

Three facts follow, none of them assumed:

1. **The current query searches full text.** OpenAlex's own echo says
   `full text has (...)`. Any long review whose body mentions omega-3 once
   qualifies — which is exactly how ESC dyslipidaemia guidelines, a ferroptosis
   review and a carotenoid paper entered the omega3 corpus.
2. **`title_and_abstract.search` still works despite being deprecated.** It
   returns results and echoes `title/abstract has (...)`.
3. **Narrowing is a ~26× reduction** on this claim (76 524 → 2 933), and the
   AND semantics are confirmed empirically: adding terms shrinks the set.

# 🟡 JUDGED — Claude's reading

Everything below is opinion formed by reading the tables above. It is
separable from them: the numbers stand whether or not this reading is right.

## The stated hypothesis is not supported

The hypothesis under test was: *abstract-less works are mostly the same junk
that search narrowing would remove anyway, so backfilling abstracts would be
wasted effort.*

**Measured: 25 of 33 (76%) carry the intervention token in their title**, so a
narrowed search would still fetch them. Only 8 of 33 would disappear. Abstract
backfill is therefore **not** made redundant by narrowing — three quarters of
the affected works would still be there, still judged on a title alone.

The hypothesis holds for one corpus only: **omega3**, where 7 of 15 abstract-less
works lack the intervention token. In the other five corpora the count is 1 of 18.

## 🛑 SUPERSEDED — the section below was written on the falsified premise

Everything from here to "Suggested order" was reasoned from titles alone. The
live variant measurement at the end of this file replaces it. It is kept
verbatim rather than deleted so the reasoning that went wrong stays auditable.

## The finding that should change the plan

Cross-referencing Q3 against the four works I earlier classed as **wrongly
excluded** (`EXCLUDED_REVIEW.md`, group B):

| wrongly-excluded work | fate under narrowing |
|---|---|
| HEALTH BENEFITS OF DOCOSAHEXAENOIC ACID (DHA) | ❌ **dropped by narrowing** |
| (n-3) Fatty Acids and Cardiovascular Health: EPA and DHA | ❌ **dropped by narrowing** |
| Effect of omega-3 … on endothelial function (meta-analysis of RCTs) | ✅ survives |
| The pros, cons, and many unknowns of probiotics | ✅ survives |

**Narrowing the search on the bare intervention term would permanently lose two
of the four works the gate currently gets wrong** — and lose them at the API,
where no local fix can recover them. Today the gate at least *sees* them, so a
synonym table can rescue them. After a naive narrowing, they never arrive.

This is the concern raised before the measurement, and the measurement confirms
it: the AND semantics are real (76 524 → 2 933 on adding terms), and neither
paper writes "omega-3" in its title, nor has an abstract to fall back on.

**Consequence: if the search is narrowed, the narrowing query must carry the
synonyms** — `title_and_abstract.search:"omega-3" OR "n-3" OR DHA OR EPA OR
"fish oil"` rather than the bare claim term. The synonym table stops being a
nice-to-have local cleanup and becomes a **precondition** of narrowing safely.
That reverses the priority I recommended in `EXCLUDED_REVIEW.md`, where I
measured the synonym table's local yield at 2 of 52 and called it low priority.
Its local yield is still 2 of 52; its value as a guard on the search change is
much higher.

## On fail-open

Fail-open (*no abstract → never exclude, mark inconclusive*) would admit 18
works today. From `EXCLUDED_REVIEW.md`'s classification of those same works,
roughly 11 were judged correctly excluded, 4 wrongly, 3 borderline — so
fail-open today buys 4 fixes at a cost of 11 admissions of off-claim material.
**I judge that a net loss at present.**

After narrowing, 8 of the 18 no longer arrive, and the residual admissions are
smaller — but two of the four fixes it was buying are among the 8 that
disappear. Fail-open gets cheaper and also less useful. **I do not think
fail-open is worth doing in either state**; it treats the symptom (no abstract)
rather than the cause, whereas backfilling the abstract removes the ambiguity
outright for 25 of 33 works.

## Suggested order

1. **Synonym table for the intervention side.** Not for its local yield, but
   because it is the precondition for narrowing the search without losing recall.
2. **Narrow the search to title+abstract, with the synonym-expanded
   intervention term** — behind a package-level switch so A/B is measurable, as
   with `picoGateEnabled` and `fullAbstractsEnabled`.
3. **Abstract backfill** for the works that still arrive without one (25 of 33
   survive narrowing). Crossref and PubMed already exist in this CLI's source
   layer.
4. **Not fail-open.**

# 🔵 MEASURED — Part 3: five search variants, live, at the real page size

The earlier "26× narrowing" figure compared *total result counts*, which decide
nothing: the CLI fetches only the top `per-page` works. What matters is whether
the **top 62** changes. Measured live on 2026-07-25, `per-page=62`, against the
omega3 corpus as it stands today.

Ground truth comes from `TestExportGateVerdicts`, which writes each work's gate
verdict to JSON with a normalized DOI. The same normalizer is applied to the
OpenAlex responses — one function, both sides, no log scraping.

**Control:** variant A must return all three works the gate currently gets wrong,
since it is the query that fetched them in the first place. It returned 3/3, so
the harness is sound. Had it not, every number below would be a measurement bug.

| variant | query | pool | gate-KEPT returned | gate-EXCLUDED returned | new | group-B |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **A** today | `search=<claim>` | 76 524 | **31/32** | **30/30** | 1 | 3/3 |
| **B** bare filter | `filter=t_a.search:omega-3` | 89 290 | 7/32 | 3/30 | 52 | 0/3 |
| **C** claim filter | `filter=t_a.search:omega-3 cardiovascular health` | 2 933 | 15/32 | 3/30 | 44 | 2/3 |
| **D** synonym OR | `filter=t_a.search:omega-3 OR DHA OR EPA OR "fish oil" OR "n-3"` | 577 924 | 5/32 | 4/30 | 53 | 2/3 |
| **E** search **+** filter | `search=<claim>` **&** `filter=t_a.search:omega-3` | **7 308** | **27/32** | **6/30** | 29 | 1/3 |

*gate-KEPT = of the 32 works the PICO gate keeps today, how many the variant
returns. gate-EXCLUDED = of the 30 it throws away, how many the variant still
fetches. Higher-left and lower-right is better.*

### A methodological finding that explains B, C and D

`sort=relevance_score:desc` **has no effect without a `search=` parameter.**
Top-5 result IDs are byte-identical with and without the sort for variants B, C
and D. Filter-only queries are therefore returned in some default order, not by
relevance — which is why their top 62 is close to arbitrary and their recall of
known-good works collapses (7/32, 15/32, 5/32).

### Which group-B work each variant recovers

Variant E returns the *omega-3 endothelial function RCT meta-analysis* but not
the DHA or (n-3) papers. Those two never write "omega-3" in their title, and
their indexed abstracts do not carry it either — B returning 0/3 on an 89 290
pool is the same effect.

# 🟡 JUDGED — corrected conclusion

**Variant E is the most promising candidate measured, not a decided answer.**

⚠️ **What E actually is: an INTERSECTION.** `search=<claim>` alone means *"full
text has (omega-3 AND improves AND cardiovascular AND health)"*.
`filter=title_and_abstract.search:omega-3` alone means *"title/abstract has
(omega-3)"*. E requires **both at once**, so it is the **narrowest** of the five
variants by construction — narrower than B, and narrower than A. Its pool of
7 308 is one tenth of A's. A variant that is strictly more restrictive will
naturally discard more noise; that is not evidence that it discards the *right*
noise, and this file has not measured what it loses relative to B.

What is measured: E cuts the works the gate has to throw away from **30 to 6**
(80% less fetched noise) while keeping **27 of the 32** the gate wants — the
best pair of numbers among the five. Mechanically that makes sense: `search=`
supplies the relevance ranking (which a filter-only query lacks entirely — see
the sort finding above), and the filter removes matches that exist only in the
full text. B, C and D each drop one of the two mechanisms and lose recall badly.

But "best of five on one corpus, on two metrics" is not "correct". E's recall
loss is already visible: 5 of the 32 gate-kept works do not come back, and two
of the three works the gate gets wrong disappear. Before E is adopted, what it
removes relative to B and to A has to be inspected by title, not just counted.

**The synonym-OR is actively harmful as a filter.** Variant D — the shape this
file originally argued was a precondition — has the *worst* recall of all five
(5/32) because ORing synonyms inflates the pool to 577 924 and the unranked
top-62 fills with generic omega-3 material. The earlier claim that a synonym
table is a precondition for narrowing is **withdrawn**. A synonym table may
still be worth having locally, at its earlier-measured yield of 2 of 52
exclusions; it is not a search-layer fix.

**The cost of E, stated plainly.** Two of the three works the gate currently
gets wrong (the DHA paper and the (n-3) EPA/DHA paper) are not in E's top 62.
Both have no abstract and neither writes "omega-3" in its title. Today the gate
at least sees them and could be taught to keep them; under E they do not arrive.
That is a real recall loss on exactly the papers a synonym table would rescue —
it is just not fixable at the filter, as D demonstrates. If those two matter,
the place to address them is a supplementary query, not a broader filter.

**Revised order:**

1. **Variant E**, behind a package-level switch, measured A/B on all 12 corpora
   — not just omega3, which is the only corpus this section covers.
2. **Re-measure the PICO gate afterwards.** If E removes 80% of what the gate
   discards, the gate's own exclusion rate should fall sharply, and the verb-gate
   widening decision should be re-taken on the new corpus rather than on this one.
3. **Abstract backfill** — unchanged in priority; it addresses works that arrive
   under any variant.
4. **Synonym table** — local only, low yield, not a precondition for anything.
5. **Not fail-open.**

**Scope warning:** every number in Part 3 is from the omega3 corpus alone.
omega3 is the worst case (48% exclusion rate, the largest corpus, the most
generic outcome terms). Variant E's benefit on saffron, meditation or probiotics
is unmeasured and should not be assumed.

# ❓ OPEN QUESTIONS — asked today, NOT measured today

Listed so nobody mistakes their absence for a null result.

1. **How many of the ~21 cardiology guidelines and generic nutrition reviews
   survive each variant?** Part 3 counts *gate-excluded works returned* (30 → 6
   for E), which is a superset of that group but not the same thing. The
   guideline-by-guideline breakdown was requested and never run.

2. **What does the synonym-OR variant (D) actually drag in?** Its top-20 titles
   were fetched once and looked clean — all omega-3 material — but the run
   crashed on a U+2010 encoding error before the list was recorded, and it was
   not repeated. D's pool is 577 924 works; the contamination question
   ("does `EPA` pull in Environmental Protection Agency papers, does `DHA` pull
   in neurology?") is **unanswered**. The `EPA` abbreviation collision is a
   specific, plausible risk that nothing here rules out.

3. **What does E lose relative to B?** E is the intersection of two conditions;
   B is one of them. The 5 gate-kept works E drops were counted, never named.
   Until they are read, "E is better" rests on two aggregate numbers.

4. **Praxvera.** The fix is reported to exist already in the Praxvera web app,
   which lives in a **separate repository** (`nejm-openalex-web`), not checked
   out here. The monorepo-wide search for `title_and_abstract` returned zero
   hits, which says nothing about Praxvera. Whether it sends the bare claim, an
   intervention-only filter, or the E-shaped intersection is **unknown**, and
   worth reading before re-deriving a design here.

5. **Deprecation timeline.** `title_and_abstract.search` is absent from the
   current OpenAlex search guide and works today. Whether and when it is removed
   was not established. Every narrowing variant except A depends on it.

6. **All corpora other than omega3.** Part 3 measured one claim. The other
   eleven are untouched.
